lead: A linear model predicts a number as a weighted sum of its inputs. Study hours go in, marks come out as ŷ = b₀ + b₁x. Least squares chooses the weights so that the squared gap between each actual y and its prediction ŷ is as small as possible. Banks score loan applicants this way, shops forecast demand from price and season, and booking sites estimate tomorrow's load from past days. The method is old, fast and readable: one closed-form answer, no training loop. This chapter builds it for one input, then for many.
prereq: You need: vectors, matrices, mean, variance and Σ notation from Unit 1, Foundations: Learning Problems and Concepts (math review).

blocks.text: Simple linear regression models one input x and one numeric output y. You have n pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ) — for example, hours studied and marks scored by n students.
ŷ = b₀ + b₁x
blocks.where: ŷ (y-hat) is the prediction; x is the input; b₀ is the intercept; b₁ is the slope.

blocks.text: b₁ is the slope: how many units ŷ moves when x rises by 1. b₀ is the intercept: the prediction when x = 0. In the worked example below, b₁ = 2 marks per hour and b₀ = 1 mark.
A real point rarely sits exactly on the line. The gap is the residual eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ. A positive residual means the model under-predicted. Write ŷ for a prediction and y for the observed value.
SSE = Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²
blocks.where: SSE is the sum of squared errors, in squared y-units; the sum runs over all n points; yᵢ is observed, ŷᵢ is predicted.

blocks.text: MSE = SSE / n
blocks.where: MSE is the mean squared error, also in squared y-units; n is the number of points.

blocks.text: With p inputs the same idea becomes multiple linear regression: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + … + bₚxₚ. Each bⱼ is the change in ŷ for a one-unit rise in xⱼ while the other inputs are held fixed. Some syllabi call this multivariate regression; the model still has one output and many inputs.
The weights b are unknown. Fitting means choosing them.

Least squares picks the b that make SSE as small as possible. Squaring does two jobs: it treats +2 and −2 errors as equally bad, and it punishes a large miss far more than a small one. Squaring also keeps the objective smooth, so calculus gives one clean answer.
b₁ = S<sub>xy</sub> / S<sub>xx</sub>,   b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄
blocks.where: S<sub>xy</sub> = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) is the cross-product sum; S<sub>xx</sub> = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²; x̄ and ȳ are the column means.

items: Compute x̄ and ȳ, the means of the two columns.
Centre every value: (xᵢ − x̄) and (yᵢ − ȳ).
Sum the products for S<sub>xy</sub>, and the squared x-gaps for S<sub>xx</sub>.
Divide: b₁ = S<sub>xy</sub> / S<sub>xx</sub>, then b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄.
Predict new points with ŷ = b₀ + b₁x.

blocks.text: Two facts fall out of the formulas. The line always passes through (x̄, ȳ), because b₀ = ȳ − b₁x̄. And S<sub>xx</sub> > 0 unless every x is identical, so a fit exists whenever x varies.
SSE is 0 when every point lies on the line and grows as the points scatter. Squared error is the default loss because it has a closed-form answer; other losses need iterative search — see 2.2.

Stack the data. Put each input row in a matrix X with a leading 1 for the intercept, the weights in a vector w, and the outputs in a vector y. All n equations then become one matrix equation: y = Xw + e.
X is n × (p+1): n rows, one column per input, plus a constant column of 1s. w is (p+1) × 1. y and e are n × 1; e holds the residuals.
SSE = (y − Xw)<sup>T</sup>(y − Xw)
blocks.where: T means transpose; the product is a 1 × 1 number, the sum of squared residuals.

blocks.text: Set the derivative of SSE with respect to w to zero. What remains is the normal equation X<sup>T</sup>Xw = X<sup>T</sup>y, solved for w:
w = (X<sup>T</sup>X)<sup>−1</sup>X<sup>T</sup>y
blocks.where: X<sup>T</sup>X is a (p+1) × (p+1) matrix that must be invertible; X<sup>T</sup>y is a (p+1) × 1 vector.

blocks.text: The inverse exists only when n ≥ p + 1 and no column is an exact linear combination of the others. A duplicated feature, or the constant column added twice, makes XTX singular. Ridge regression adds λI and repairs it — see 2.6.

Polynomial regression fits y = b₀ + b₁x + b₂x² + … . You build extra columns x², x³ from the same x. The curve is not linear in x, but it is linear in the weights, so it is still linear regression and the normal equation is unchanged. Some syllabi call this curvilinear regression.

The inverse costs about O(p³), which is fine for hundreds of features and too slow for millions; there you minimise SSE by gradient descent instead (2.2). One short note: when a model is nonlinear in the weights themselves, least squares has no closed form and needs iterative search. Only a few universities teach that under the name nonlinear least squares.

figure.caption: For the three shops, SSE is lowest at slope b₁ = 1, about 0.6667 units². With b₀ = 2/3, the least-squares line is ŷ = 0.6667 + x.

spec.aria: A U-shaped curve of SSE against slope b1 for the three shops, with its lowest point marked at b1 = 1 and SSE = 0.6667 units squared.

examples.question: Five students studied x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 hours and scored y = 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 marks. (a) Fit the least-squares line ŷ = b₀ + b₁x. (b) Predict the marks for 6 hours of study. (c) State SSE.
steps: b₁ = S<sub>xy</sub> / S<sub>xx</sub> = 20/10 = 2 marks per hour.
Line: marks = 2 × hours + 1. At x = 6 hours, ŷ = 2 × 6 + 1 = 13 marks.
Every point lies on the line, so each residual is 0 and SSE = 0 marks².
examples.answer: marks = 2 × hours + 1, predicting 13 marks at 6 hours, with SSE = 0.
examples.check:
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
y = [3, 5, 7, 9, 11]
n = len(x)
mx = sum(x) / n
my = sum(y) / n
sxy = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
sxx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x)
b1 = sxy / sxx
b0 = my - b1 * mx
pred = b0 + b1 * 6
sse = sum((b - (b0 + b1 * a)) ** 2 for a, b in zip(x, y))
print(b1)
print(b0)
print(pred)
print(sse)

examples.question: Three shops spent x = 1, 2, 3 thousand rupees on ads and sold y = 2, 2, 4 units. Fit ŷ = b₀ + b₁x, then compute SSE and MSE.
steps: Means: x̄ = (1+2+3)/3 = 2 thousand rupees; ȳ = (2+2+4)/3 = 8/3 ≈ 2.6667 units.
examples.answer: ŷ = 0.6667 + 1 × x, with SSE ≈ 0.6667 units² and MSE ≈ 0.2222 units².
examples.check:
x = [1, 2, 3]
y = [2, 2, 4]
n = len(x)
mx = sum(x) / n
my = sum(y) / n
sxy = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
sxx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x)
b1 = sxy / sxx
b0 = my - b1 * mx
sse = sum((b - (b0 + b1 * a)) ** 2 for a, b in zip(x, y))
mse = sse / n
print(round(b1, 4))
print(round(b0, 4))
print(round(sse, 4))
print(round(mse, 4))

traps: Swapping the columns: S<sub>xy</sub> uses x-gaps times y-gaps. If you regress x on y instead of y on x you get a different line, with slope S<sub>xy</sub>/S<sub>yy</sub>.
Dropping the constant column of 1s from X. Without it the line is forced through the origin, b₀ vanishes and the fit is no longer least squares with an intercept.
Reading SSE as MSE. SSE is a raw sum that grows with n; divide by n before comparing models on different numbers of points.
Claiming a good model from a high R² on training data. Overfitting can produce it, and extrapolating far outside the observed x is unsafe.
Calling a polynomial fit nonlinear regression. It is linear in the weights, so the normal equation still applies; nonlinear least squares means nonlinearity in the weights.

quiz.q: In ŷ = b₀ + b₁x, what do b₀ and b₁ mean?
quiz.a: b₁ is the slope, the change in the prediction for a one-unit rise in x. b₀ is the intercept, the prediction when x = 0.

quiz.q: Write SSE and MSE for n points.
quiz.a: SSE = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² and MSE = SSE/n. Both are in squared y-units.

quiz.q: Why does least squares square the residuals instead of taking absolute values?
quiz.a: Squaring treats positive and negative errors alike and punishes large misses more than small ones. It also keeps the objective smooth and differentiable, which is what gives the closed-form b₁ = S<sub>xy</sub>/S<sub>xx</sub>.

quiz.q: For x = 2, 4, 6, 8 and y = 3, 5, 9, 11, find the least-squares line.
Write the design matrix rows for a quadratic fit ŷ = b₀ + b₁x + b₂x² on the points x = 1 and x = 2.
quiz.a: Row for x = 1: [1, 1, 1]. Row for x = 2: [1, 2, 4]. The three columns are the constant, x and x², and the model is still linear in the weights.

quiz.q: A model reports R² = 0.98 on training data but predicts badly on new data. Give two likely causes and one fix.
quiz.a: Overfitting to noise, usually from too many features for the number of rows, and extrapolation outside the observed x range. Fix by holding out data or cross-validating, reducing features, or adding a ridge penalty.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real libraries rarely invert X<sup>T</sup>X directly; they solve the normal equation with QR or Cholesky factorisation, which is numerically safer. Weighted least squares handles points with unequal noise, and generalised least squares handles correlated errors. Ridge is exactly the normal equation with λI added to the matrix, and the kernel trick turns it into kernel ridge regression for curved fits. Search for 'normal equation QR decomposition', 'weighted least squares' and 'scikit-learn LinearRegression' to go further.
